raw_text:
The introduction of drug-eluting stents (DES) revolutionized percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) by dramatically reducing restenosis. However, permanent caging of the coronary vessel by metallic stents restricts vasomotion, prevents adaptive positive remodeling, and presents a lifelong risk of very late stent thrombosis. To overcome these limitations, the paradigm of "vascular restorative therapy" was introduced. This concept envisioned using temporary mechanical support that subsequently resorbs, liberating the vessel and leaving no permanent hardware behind. The technology developed to fulfill this promise is the bioresorbable vascular scaffold (BVS).

The earliest clinical feasibility of a polymer-based BVS was evaluated with the poly-L-lactic acid (PLLA)-based, everolimus-eluting Absorb BVS (Abbott Vascular) in first-in-human cohorts, specifically the ABSORB Cohort A [1] and Cohort B [2] trials. Promising early angiographic and optical coherence tomography (OCT) findings catalyzed larger randomized trials. The pivotal ABSORB III trial [3] demonstrated one-year non-inferiority of the Absorb BVS compared to metallic everolimus-eluting stents (EES) in terms of target lesion failure (TLF). This was corroborated by other international programs, including the ABSORB II [4], ABSORB China [5], and ABSORB Japan [6] randomized controlled trials, which demonstrated acceptable short-term clinical and angiographic performance. To validate BVS in routine, unselected clinical practice, the ABSORB IV trial [7] and the all-comers AIDA trial [8] were initiated.

Despite high initial enthusiasm, mid- to long-term clinical trial data revealed a troubling signal of increased adverse events. A landmark patient-level pooled meta-analysis of the ABSORB trials by Ali et al. [9] confirmed a significantly higher risk of TLF and scaffold thrombosis (ScT) through three years of follow-up. Five-year data from the ABSORB III trial [10] showed that while clinical event rates stabilized after the period of complete scaffold resorption (around three years), the early deficit compared to metallic EES was never fully recovered. Long-term results from the ABSORB IV [11] and final five-year results of the AIDA trial [12] reinforced this concern, documenting significantly higher cumulative rates of device thrombosis. High-restenosis-risk cohorts evaluated in the COMPARE-ABSORB trial also demonstrated worse clinical outcomes [13], leading to the premature termination of its enrolment, with final seven-year results showing sustained higher event rates in the BVS cohort [14]. Evaluation of first-generation PLLA scaffolds in acute coronary syndromes similarly showed disappointing results, as demonstrated in the ISAR-Absorb MI trial [15] and the first-generation magnesium-based scaffold in the MAGSTEMI trial [16], although the five-year results of the MAGSTEMI trial did show restoration of physiological vasomotion in successfully healed vessels [17].

Pathophysiological and intracoronary imaging investigations linked these failures to key device design features and procedural parameters. Scaffolds suffered from mechanical fragility, lower tensile strength, and thick struts (~150 µm) that disrupted laminar blood flow, predisposing the segment to flow stagnation, endothelial dysfunction, and platelet activation, as thoroughly assessed by Puricel et al. [18]. Recognizing these drawbacks, clinical experts established the "PSP" protocol (Prepare the lesion, Size appropriately, Post-dilate with non-compliant balloons) [19] to optimize BVS expansion and minimize malapposition. Despite technique optimization, the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) and European Association of Percutaneous Cardiovascular Interventions (EAPCI) Task Force consensus [20] advised against using first-generation BVS in unselected routine PCI.

To overcome the limitations of first-generation polymeric scaffolds, next-generation devices have focused on alternative materials and ultra-thin strut designs. The second-generation sirolimus-eluting resorbable magnesium scaffold (Magmaris; Biotronik) featured a metallic backbone with faster resorption kinetics (approximately 12 months) and demonstrated good safety profiles in the prospective BIOSOLVE-II trial [21] and the large-scale BIOSOLVE-IV registry [22]. Building on this platform, the third-generation sirolimus-eluting resorbable magnesium scaffold (Freesolve/DREAMS 3G) was developed, featuring thinner struts (99 µm) and improved radial strength, which yielded promising one-year safety and efficacy outcomes in the BIOMAG-I trial [23].

Concurrently, PLLA-based polymeric technology has evolved with thinner struts. The MeRes100 sirolimus-eluting BRS (100 µm struts) demonstrated positive three-year clinical and multimodality imaging results in the MeRes-1 trial [24], suggesting that thinner polymer struts enhance deliverability and vessel healing. Similarly, the thin-strut Firesorb BRS (100–125 µm struts) demonstrated acceptable one-year angiographic late lumen loss and fast strut coverage in the FUTURE-II trial [25].

Real-world registries like GHOST-EU [26] and randomized trials like TROFI II [27] initially provided critical insights into patient selection and the vascular healing response of BVS, helping define the limits of the technology. As summarized in comprehensive reviews [28], early-generation failures should not overshadow the potential of this technology. Alternative next-generation thin-strut designs, such as the novolimus-eluting DESolve scaffold [29] and the tyrosine-polycarbonate-based Fantom scaffold [30], have further validated the feasibility of transient coronary caging.

In conclusion, the first generation of bioresorbable vascular scaffolds fell short of expectations due to suboptimal mechanical profiles (specifically thick struts) and incomplete implantation techniques. However, the paradigm of vascular restoration remains highly desirable. With the advent of third-generation ultra-thin resorbable metallic and polymeric scaffolds, optimized implantation techniques, and mandatory intravascular imaging guidance, bioresorbable technology is poised for a major comeback in percutaneous coronary revascularization.
